label: Tangent Space, Nonsingularity, and Dimension
notes: Open the chapter. We bring calculus into algebraic geometry. The deck follows printed pages 101 through 108 and develops the Zariski tangent space, the notion of a nonsingular point, the definition of dimension, and the theorem that a point is smooth exactly when its tangent space has the expected dimension, tying local and global pictures together.

label: The Tangent Space
notes: Define the Zariski tangent space at a point as the linear space cut out by the differentials of the defining equations. This is the algebraic version of the tangent plane from calculus, computed purely with the Jacobian matrix. It measures the first-order behavior of the variety near the point without any reference to limits.

label: Nonsingular Points
notes: Call a point nonsingular, or smooth, when the tangent space has the smallest possible dimension, equal to the dimension of the variety. Equivalently the Jacobian attains full rank there. Singular points, where the tangent space jumps up, are exactly the places where the variety fails to be locally like affine space, such as cusps and nodes.

label: Dimension
notes: Define the dimension of a variety algebraically, as the length of the longest chain of irreducible subvarieties, matching the transcendence degree of its function field. For nice varieties this agrees with intuition: a curve is one-dimensional, a surface two. Dimension is a birational invariant and the most basic numerical measure of size.

label: Smoothness and the Jacobian
notes: State the smoothness criterion. A point is nonsingular precisely when the rank of the Jacobian equals the codimension, so the tangent space dimension equals the dimension of the variety. The singular locus is itself a closed subvariety, cut out by the vanishing of the relevant minors, and is generically empty for an irreducible variety.

label: Recap
notes: Close the chapter. The Zariski tangent space linearizes a variety at a point, nonsingularity means the tangent space has the expected dimension, dimension is measured by chains of subvarieties or transcendence degree, and the Jacobian criterion detects smoothness. With local structure understood, the final chapter counts the twenty-seven lines on a cubic surface.
